interactions.label: Which mechanism maintains lens transparency by preventing damaged proteins from

params.question: Which mechanism maintains lens transparency by preventing damaged proteins from aggregating?

answers.text: Reduced glutathione scavenging free radicals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reduced glutathione does protect the lens, but its role is neutralising oxidative damage — not directly preventing protein aggregation. That chaperone function belongs to alpha-crystallin.

answers.text: Alpha-crystallin acting as a molecular chaperone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Alpha-crystallin binds to partially denatured lens proteins and prevents them from clumping into light-scattering aggregates — a true chaperone function distinct from the other two transparency mechanisms.

answers.text: Sodium-potassium pump maintaining ionic gradient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Na/K-ATPase maintains a compact, low-water state in lens fibres — essential for transparency — but it does not prevent protein aggregation. That is alpha-crystallin's chaperone function.

answers.text: Aqueous humour continuously washing the lens surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aqueous humour nourishes the avascular lens, but it does not directly prevent protein aggregation within the lens fibres. The intracellular chaperone that prevents damaged proteins from clumping is alpha-crystallin.

overallFeedback.feedback: Alpha-crystallin acts as a molecular chaperone, binding to damaged proteins and preventing aggregation — a distinct role from the Na/K pump (ionic gradient) and glutathione (antioxidant defence). When any of these three fails, proteins clump, light scatters, and cataract begins.
Alpha-crystallin is one of three key mechanisms maintaining lens transparency, alongside the Na/K pump (low-water state) and reduced glutathione (antioxidant defence).

interactions.label: A 70-year-old patient with a longstanding dense white cataract presents with sud

params.question: A 70-year-old patient with a longstanding dense white cataract presents with sudden pain, redness, and raised intraocular pressure. Open-angle examination shows no pupillary block. What is the most likely mechanism?

answers.text: Swollen intumescent lens pushing the iris forward, closing the drainage angle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes phacomorphic glaucoma, which occurs with a swollen lens and produces angle closure. However, the question specifies an open angle with no pupillary block, ruling out this mechanism.

answers.text: Posterior synechiae from chronic anterior uveitis obstructing aqueous outflow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic uveitis can cause secondary glaucoma, but the clinical picture here — a longstanding dense cataract with open angles — points to phacolytic glaucoma from leaked lens proteins, not an inflammatory aetiology.

answers.text: Leaked lens proteins attracting macrophages that clog the trabecular meshwork

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract, the liquefied cortex leaks high-molecular-weight proteins through the intact capsule. Macrophages engulf these proteins and physically block the trabecular meshwork, causing phacolytic glaucoma — an open-angle mechanism.

answers.text: Neovascular membrane growing over the trabecular meshwork

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neovascular glaucoma results from retinal ischaemia (e.g., diabetic retinopathy, central retinal vein occlusion), not from a hypermature cataract. The open-angle mechanism here is macrophage clogging from leaked lens proteins.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a hypermature lens, the cortex liquefies and leaks proteins through the intact capsule. Macrophages loaded with these proteins physically block the trabecular meshwork, causing phacolytic glaucoma — an open-angle mechanism distinct from the angle-closure of phacomorphic glaucoma.
Phacolytic glaucoma is a sight-threatening complication of hypermature cataract that requires urgent lens extraction to eliminate the source of protein leakage.

interactions.label: During pre-operative counselling, a patient asks whether the cataract can 'come

params.question: During pre-operative counselling, a patient asks whether the cataract can 'come back' after surgery. Which response is most appropriate?

answers.text: Yes, cataract can return after five to ten years and will need repeat surgery.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is incorrect and would cause unnecessary anxiety. An artificial intraocular lens does not develop cataract. What patients sometimes call 'return of cataract' is posterior capsule opacification, treated with a simple outpatient laser — not repeat surgery.

answers.text: Recurrence depends entirely on your blood sugar control; strict control prevents it.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diabetes can accelerate cataract formation in the natural lens, but once the lens is replaced with an artificial one, blood sugar control does not cause the IOL to cloud. PCO may occur regardless of glycaemic status.

answers.text: Cataract never recurs; the artificial lens is permanent and nothing else can cloud.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the artificial lens itself cannot cloud, this answer omits posterior capsule opacification, which occurs in up to 20–30% of patients. Telling a patient nothing can cloud may undermine trust if PCO develops later.

answers.text: The artificial lens cannot cloud, but the membrane behind it may opacify and is easily treated with a laser procedure.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Posterior capsule opacification is not cataract recurrence — the intraocular lens remains clear. A brief outpatient Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy restores vision. Explaining this distinction is a key element of informed counselling.

overallFeedback.feedback: Posterior capsule opacification is not the cataract returning — the artificial lens cannot cloud. A brief outpatient Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy clears the membrane. This distinction must be explained during pre-operative counselling to ensure informed consent.
Addressing the PCO misconception is one of the six essential counselling elements before cataract surgery, alongside diagnosis, technique, anaesthesia, risks, and realistic expectations.

interactions.label: Three days after cataract surgery, a patient develops increasing pain, redness,

params.question: Three days after cataract surgery, a patient develops increasing pain, redness, and decreasing vision. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

answers.text: Administer intravitreal antibiotics and refer for vitreoretinal evaluation the same day

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Post-cataract pain, redness, and declining vision is endophthalmitis until proven otherwise. Intravitreal antibiotics must be given the same day. Delay significantly worsens visual outcomes.

answers.text: Prescribe oral antibiotics and review after 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral antibiotics alone are inadequate for suspected endophthalmitis. The vitreous cavity is poorly penetrated by systemic antibiotics. Intravitreal injection delivers therapeutic drug levels directly to the site of infection and must not be delayed.

answers.text: Increase the frequency of topical prednisolone acetate drops

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Increasing steroids without addressing a likely infection would be dangerous. Pain, redness, and falling vision after cataract surgery is endophthalmitis until proven otherwise — it requires intravitreal antibiotics, not immunosuppression alone.

answers.text: Perform Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy to rule out posterior capsule opacification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PCO is a late complication developing over months to years, not days. The acute triad of pain, redness, and falling vision in the early postoperative period points to endophthalmitis, which demands immediate intravitreal antibiotics.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pain, redness, and falling vision after day one is endophthalmitis until proven otherwise. The standard of care is same-day intravitreal antibiotics with immediate vitreoretinal referral — never reassure and wait.
The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study showed that prompt intravitreal antibiotics are critical, and vitrectomy improves outcomes when presenting vision is light perception or worse.

interactions.label: A 2-year-old child undergoes unilateral cataract extraction without intraocular

params.question: A 2-year-old child undergoes unilateral cataract extraction without intraocular lens implantation. Which optical correction is most appropriate at this stage?

answers.text: Aphakic spectacles with plus ten dioptre lenses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aphakic spectacles magnify the image by 25–30%. In unilateral aphakia, this creates intolerable aniseikonia exceeding the 5% fusion limit between the two eyes. Spectacles are contraindicated for unilateral aphakia.

answers.text: Immediate secondary intraocular lens implantation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In a growing eye, accurate IOL power calculation is unreliable because the axial length and refractive state will shift significantly. IOL implantation is deferred until the eye has stabilised, typically in later childhood.

answers.text: Silicone contact lens with amblyopia therapy on the fellow eye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A contact lens reduces magnification to about 7%, acceptable even for unilateral aphakia. Simultaneous patching of the fellow eye is critical to prevent deprivation amblyopia during the sensitive period of visual development. IOL follows once the eye stabilises.

answers.text: No correction until the child is old enough for a reliable refraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Leaving the eye uncorrected risks irreversible deprivation amblyopia. The visual cortex requires focused input during the critical period of development. Early optical correction with a contact lens, combined with amblyopia therapy, is essential.

overallFeedback.feedback: In paediatric unilateral aphakia, a contact lens provides optical correction with acceptable magnification (~7%), while simultaneous patching of the fellow eye prevents deprivation amblyopia. IOL implantation is deferred until the eye stops growing.
The stepwise approach for paediatric unilateral aphakia is: contact lens for immediate optical correction, patching for amblyopia, and IOL implantation once the eye has stabilised.
